Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the author's and Scooter's companion on rock-throwing expeditions to Gus Haigner's and the lumber shed, and photographed with a sheepherder's burro named Dynamite.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" among the boys spellbound by Tanana Cimarron's campfire stories, one of the group with cowboy chaps in "Cowboys and Gentlemen," and photographed in "The Ranch Hands" with Scooter, Joey, and Raymond Lane.

Named in Chapter III of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the author's partner in a puppet-class scandal sculpting Principal Bogue, and present, with Grandma Lane, for Witt Thomas's mare's difficult foaling.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Let's Hear That One Again"; pictured holding the reins of "Old Dynamite," a white burro, and shared bandanna neckerchiefs and Bull Durham smoking sessions with David Manning behind Mortensen's shed.

Named again as "Lee Davis" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Memories"; one of "The Dragon Slayers of Moonshine Mesa," photographed in 1929 with Scooter Jackson, Joel Jackson, Frank Davis and Raymond Lane.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Geologist Seeks Ore With Fly Rod and Reel"; with the author, wasted a box of .25-20 shells shooting at rock rabbits in Sawmill Gulch in the mid-1930s, then spun an elaborate false deer-hunting tale for his father, Uncle Frank.

Named in the Acknowledgments of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as his wife, sweetheart and companion "who has tried so valiantly to reform me."

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Hard Water"; weathered the last freezeup with the author in the winter of 1966-67, undone by a neighbor's hibernating pet groundhog.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Twice Around the Barber Pole"; has cut the author’s hair for over 40 years, opening only one wound in that time a butterfly patch couldn’t close.
Named at length in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Decibels Unlimited"; the author’s account of a drunken New Year’s Eve drive home, and of a later, jarringly loud Elks Hall dance.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Doc Leary Battles Handicap"; shown off trophies with Mike McClure and Gene Wardell at a Rocky Mountain Regional Archery tournament.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Silver Tongue Oil No Help With Poetry"; joined Jackie Wyatt in sampling "silver tongue oil" on a visit to Cebolla Creek.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "New Year’s Greetings"; the vacuum-cleaner routine that ends every argument in the author’s favor, or so he claims.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Wisdom of Age"; the two-day yard sale that sold off years of accumulated "treasures."
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "A Present for Mary"; on the receiving end of Lucy the cat's prize live mouse, delivered to the living room.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Separate Beds"; the whole piece is a tall-tale account of a mock "trial separation" touched off by an anniversary chain saw.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Smooth as a Biscuit"; found a dead mouse in the ranch's water sump.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Old Tom Just Never Could Adjust to Retirement Life"; cried alongside the author when their old tomcat was put down.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Family Feud Follows Forgetfulness"; the whole piece is a tall-tale account of an anniversary argument, including the author's account of injuring her hand in a door in 1951.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "Brush With Trooper Recalls Law's Rare Visits to Creede"; waits on the lawn, armed with a poker and ball bat, when John comes home after the wreck.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "Housecleaning Is a Breeze When Done Jackson's Way"; misreads John's digging in the garden as burying her mistakenly "deceased" father, Paul Schriver.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "You Get Caught Doing Darndest Stuff"; rushes her father Paul to the hospital after the oxygen-line mix-up.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "Hopeful Wife Can Be Trying"; reads seed catalogs by the wood heater on a subzero morning while John clears a watering hole for the cattle.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "Wife Is All Thumbs"; the central figure of this story about a temperamental vacuum cleaner and sewing machine.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Thundermug John Apologizes to His Friends, Family — Almost"; gave her husband a stern lecture on relaxation techniques during his "enforced sabbatical," deflected by his reminder of a wilder version of himself thirty years earlier.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Paul's Recipe"; kept the author posted, during his travels, on her father Paul's expanding garden "recipe" and its casualties, real and invented.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; co-honoree, with the author, of Toni Shaw's surprise "Happy Birthday" party.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Dog a Big Help on Prospecting Expedition"; packed Skeeter's ziplock bag of Kibbles and Bits and meat scraps for a prospecting trip.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Geologist Seeks Ore With Fly Rod and Reel"; fielded office calls covering for the author's unexplained field absences with invented quad names.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Lower Roost for In-Laws"; the whole piece is a tall-tale account of her return from a leave of absence, including her own theory linking in-laws and relatives.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; the title story's central figure, drawing blood rather than a fish while ice fishing with the author on Blue Mesa Lake.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Marriages Weather Storms With Love"; the author's own marriage to her is held up, in this piece, against his parents' quieter, harder-to-read one.
Addressed by the handwritten inscription on the title page of the scanned copy of "Who Upset the Thunder Mug" as "the love of my life" and "my beautiful Inie," signed "Your old Thundermug."

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Wedding Bells and Chesapeake Retrievers"; John's wedding to Inez, told as a surprise marriage before a Spanish-speaking Justice of the Peace with the Sheriff of Taos County as witness, "well over 40 years" before the book; she then helped choose their first registered Chesapeake Retriever puppy.
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Let Me Put It Another Way"; as "Inez," who arrived at the Elk's bar to take home a very drunk John while "a perturbed husband" looked on.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Records Were Made To Be Broken"; as John's "bride" and "the little gal from Kansas," in a story of early married life in a one-room cabin, a bridal shower in the old Red Cross Hall, and a photograph captioned "Inez M. Jackson and Skeeter."

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Purse Your Lips Before You Blow"; as "Mrs. Jackson" and "my bride," scolding John after meetings of the "Upper Willow Creek Mineralogical Society and Glee Club" and trimming the gray hair in his ears.

Named as "Inie" in "Old Tom was Color Blind," Chapter II of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; her husband's embarrassment when their black tomcat coughs up a telltale blue feather after her sidewalk mishap.

Named as "Inez Jackson" in "Synopsis," Chapter VI of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," captioned "Trainer, Inez Jackson and Author (at obedience school)"; also worried, elsewhere in the same chapter, about the author's bowel habits in "The Golden Years."

Named in "'Long Distance Indigestion,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear"; a 19-year-old bride startled by an unannounced, long-winded visitor who commandeered the telephone and, eventually, a cup of coffee.
Named in "Marriage Is a Partnership," Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear"; credited with perfecting "several methods to control" John's "errant behavior."
Pictured and named in the Dedication, the book's actual final page, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear"; John's wife, to whom the book is dedicated, "Because I Love You, That's Why!"

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of," the memorial her grandson John dedicated to her and her husband William; the book gives her birthplace as Stockholm, Sweden, which does not match the site's own primary-source research placing her birth in Bjurtjärn (or possibly Bjurkärna) parish, Värmland — flagged, not resolved, on this page.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "A Wake for Herb"; as Herbert "Pee Wee" Hutchinson, the "victim" of the mock killing and its wake, a good dancer and reciter of "The Ballad of Dan McGrew"; also pictured seated on a '39 Ford.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "I'll Drink to That (Or Anything Else)"; second at left in a bar photograph with Ray Ball, Lucky Keene, Archie "Spud" Fellows and bartender Ed Hargraves.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Wintertime Travelling Is Not for Us"; recalled thirty-six years earlier marveling, with Bertha Larson and Lucille Wilson, at the view of the Great Salt Lake basin, since obscured by smog.

Named in John Jackson's 1988 tribute to Joel; foreman under whom Joel worked as a hard-rock miner at the Commodore tunnels

Named in John Jackson's memoir "Please Go to Hell"; married Anna Maud after buying the old Gardnier homestead, where they ran a firewood and mine-prop business
Referred to only as "my grandfather" in John Jackson's account of the Snowshoe Mountain moonshiners; identified through family knowledge (27 Aug 2026) as Charles Lane.

Called "Granddad Lane" throughout Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," in "Grandparents, the Building Blocks"; a wood and mine-prop supplier on his 160-acre Moonshine Mesa homestead, remembered for wild wagon rides after too much time in Phillips Beer Parlor, folksy wisdom about not making "a brood mare out of a good riding horse," and standing armed guard over his grain fields each June against passing sheep herds with his 30-30 Winchester.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five" as the author's best pal and confidant at five years old; gave him his first rifle and was with him at age ten for an out-of-season bull elk kill to stock the larder.

Named as "Granddad Lane" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Never Bet a Cinch"; sawing blocks from Red Spruce logs with the author when Al Hibbs and Arthur Davis drove in, and staked the dime for Al's shooting-contest bet.
Named again as "Grandad Lane" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Hard Water"; hauled water from the Rio Grande in wooden barrels behind his team, Shorty and Chubby.

Named again as "Granddad Lane" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Two," in "Short Stuff"; hauling firewood from the Lane ranch on Moonshine Mesa with young John when Roy LaFont stopped to admire a loose wheel rim.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "Granddad and the Jayhawker"; appears as "Granddad" and, once, as "Mr. Lane," John's step-grandfather, delivering firewood with the boy to summer residents at Idlewild on the road to Spar City and refusing to be beaten down on the price.
Child of Anna Maud Woodruff and Robert Abraham Lincoln Davis

Called "Uncle Frank Davis" in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; married to "Aunt Caroline," whose kitchen and homemade bread the author visited often, and photographed with her and two of their children, Polly and Nancy.
Named as "Frank Davis" in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; Alex Duncan moved to a house across the gulch from him.

Named as "Uncle Frank" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Geologist Seeks Ore With Fly Rod and Reel"; entrusted his rifle and skinning knife to a young John and Lee Davis for a hard-times-season rabbit hunt in the mid-1930s, then nearly walked them back out to "finish" a deer they'd invented. Husband of the site's existing Aunt Caroline, father of Lee Davis and of the site's existing Frank Davis, Jr.
Child of Anna Maud Woodruff and Robert Abraham Lincoln Davis; per family account, later Rose Davis Cook (unconfirmed)

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "Who Upset the Thundermug"; probably "Rose," the eldest daughter, courted by a handsome local cowboy until the thundermug spilled on them; per family account Edna Rosamond went by Rose, though this is not confirmed.

Known to family as "Uncle Woody"; named in his nephew John Jackson's memoir "Please Go to Hell" — stayed with the Jackson family in the early 1930s, teaching Joel a riddle that nearly got him expelled from school. Identified through family knowledge as the same person.

Called "Uncle Woodruff Davis" and "Uncle Woody" in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; built Joel a beanie flipper from a forked willow limb and inner tube rubber, which Joel used to spook the Allen sisters' dairy herd.

Called "Uncle Woody" in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; bypassed the family's electric meter and learned to roll back its kilowatt-hour reading, to town electrician Ivan Weaver's chagrin.

Named as "Uncle Woodie" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; with Uncle Art, taught Joey Jackson the rabbit's-hole riddle he tried on his teacher — the same story, differently detailed, as Chapter III of "Once Around the Thunder Mug."

Named as "Art" in John Jackson's memoir "Please Go to Hell"; recalled with Frankie Davis among the old friends and "pards" on John's imagined Memory Lane bus ride. Identified through family knowledge as this same Arthur M. Davis.

Named as "Uncle Arthur" in Chapter III of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; recited the rabbit's-hole riddle that Joey repeated to his teacher, Christine Duncan. Identified through family knowledge as Alice Josephine Davis's ("Mom Jo"'s) brother, this same Arthur M. Davis.

Named as "Uncle Art" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; with Uncle Woodie, taught Joey Jackson the rabbit's-hole riddle he tried on teacher Miss Marie Birdsey — the same story credited to "Uncle Arthur" alone in Chapter III of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," there recited to Christine Duncan.

Named as "Art" and "Arthur Davis" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Never Bet a Cinch"; joined Al Hibbs on an unscheduled prairie-dog-shooting holiday, competing against the author in a marksmanship demonstration.

Second wife of Robert Abraham Lincoln Davis; married 8 Jul 1931, Neosho, Missouri, per a marriage license located since this entry was first written — no longer unverified. Robert's own death certificate lists her as his wife at his 1943 death.

Almost certainly the "Cora Dear" named in Robert’s poem "Womans Love" — per Robert’s own note, written years earlier for a widow he was courting who didn’t believe he’d written it himself, and whom he went on to marry regardless.

Named as "Charlotte McClure" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Women Can Scare Strongest Man"; John McClure’s wife, shared lunch with the author at his Cebolla Creek home the day Bea Jean Wintz stormed in.

Wrote the poem "Getting Even," reproduced here in full under her own byline. Per family knowledge, the newspaper's owner at the time refused to print it and accused her, in a poison-pen letter, of trying to destroy her brother's reputation; a later owner found the letters years afterward and published the poem without asking either sibling first. Also embedded, with an editor's note, in her brother John's 1997 collection "Echoes from the Thundermug," under his own column heading, "For Love of a Brother." Living; identifying details withheld as elsewhere on the site.

Named as "Polly Bates" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; with husband Lucky, drove in for the author and Inez's surprise birthday party. A nickname variant for this site's existing Pauline Roberta "Bubbles" Jackson Bates, in her own brother's words. Per family knowledge, Bubbles was known by that name to family, friends, and the wider community her whole life; when she married, her husband's family considered "Bubbles" improper and called her Pauline or Polly instead, so both parents were known growing up through various combinations — Jerry/Lucky and Bubbles/Pauline/Polly — depending on who was speaking. Curiously, John himself used "Lucky" and "Bubbles" everywhere else, per family knowledge; why he chose "Polly" here, in print, isn't clear — left as an open question rather than guessed at. Distinct from this site's other "Polly," first cousin Anna Maude "Polly" Davis (daughter of Uncle Frank Davis, Jo's brother); per family knowledge, Shannon's father Lucky is not believed to have met cousin Polly, and the passage names "Polly Bates" — Pauline's married surname — so this appearance is confidently Shannon's mother, not the cousin.

Named as "Charlie Matson" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inside Plumbing Blesses Creede"; Dad Bill's well beneath an enclosed porch served his and Ed Snow's households.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; returned to his claims on West Willow Creek after wintering in Arizona. No confirmed relation to Bob Oates, also named on this site.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; with his wife Pinky and sons Dale and Emmett, ran a dairy near Sunnyside road and Road 149, delivering milk to town by sleigh in winter.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the Creede milkman the author mistook, as a small boy, for his own father after overhearing an adult joke.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; had to park his milk-delivery team and sleigh and finish his rounds on foot when the mesa road grew too icy from sledding.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug", wife of Frank Bruns and mother of Dale and Emmett, ran the family dairy near Sunnyside road and Road 149.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug", son of Frank and Pinky Bruns.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug", son of Frank and Pinky Bruns.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a runaway milk sleigh nearly reached his place before Frank Bruns's team tired out in deep snow.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; with his wife Annie, took honors for the largest and most varied garden in Creede, and shared milk and vegetables from their Holstein cows with neighbors.
Named with his wife Annie in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; puzzled over his milk cows' contrariness on days when local kids had been secretly riding them.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; with her husband Charles, took honors for the largest and most varied garden in Creede.
Named with her husband Charles in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the couple's milk cows pastured where mill tailing dams now stand.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as Creede's Forest Ranger and Game Warden, who "never intruded as long as there was no waste of meat" on families supplementing their tables with deer and elk.

Very likely the unnamed "Forest Ranger and Game Warden turned firefighter" in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," who came home from the mercantile-block fire to a wife swinging a skillet at his face — though the book does not name him directly in this passage.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Boxers Highlighted Old Traveling Circuses"; sparred, trained and coached Creede's boxing team with Pete Bruns.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Memories"; pictured as a forest ranger and game warden.

Named (surname only) in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; ran a sprawling livery building and shop north of the telephone office where a horse could still be shod as cars replaced horse-drawn transportation.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; kept two teams and ore wagons in service in 1920s Creede. No confirmed relation to Byron, Annie, or Clinton Fairchild, also named on this site.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Mule Skinners of 40-Years Ago Were a Hardy Breed"; one of the Emperius Mining Co. skinners during the author's first years there.
Named as "Art Fairchild" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Jackson Recalls Building of Ore Bins"; one of the last Creede teamsters, skidded rail for the Commodore 5 tunnel with his own team.

Quoted, as "Art Fairchild," in "Third Stool from the Rear," "From the Barrel of Common Sense," page iv, explaining why Creede Transportation Company could pay a dollar more per shift than the mining companies.
Named as "Art Fairchild" in an untitled barroom vignette, Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 3; the only thing that scares him is his wife Cora "on the peck."

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the engineer supervising the clay mine, hauling bentonite by truck to a self-loading tipple near Frank Powell's home. No confirmed relation to Fred "Soapy," Sam, Garnet, or Norman Birdsey, also named on this site.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the clay mine's self-loading tipple, supervised by Ben A. Birdsey, stood near his home. No confirmed relation to Donald Powell, also named on this site.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Stealing Ain't As Easy As It Was In Times Past"; a trucker hauled scrap ore from the mine to a loading dock near his home.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Toils and Foibles of the Depression Kid"; operated the grader on Mineral County's road crew.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; Sheriff over Bill Jackson's role as Undersheriff, at the time of a moonshiners' shooting feud over a plugged irrigation ditch.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the sheriff over Bill Jackson's post as Undersheriff, during the moonshiners' shooting feud between Mr. Arlow and a rival.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the man Dad Bill served as undersheriff to for several years — the source of the .45 revolver Dad Bill carried on the family's Missouri road trip.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Ozark Adventures" — the same road trip, differently detailed, as Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the source of the .45 revolver Dad Bill carried on the family's Missouri road trip.

Named (surname only) in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; plugged a rival moonshiner's irrigation ditch, touching off a rifle-fire feud across a canyon that Undersheriff Bill Jackson had to intervene in.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; plugged a rival moonshiner's irrigation ditch, touching off a rifle-fire feud that Bill Jackson, as Undersheriff, had to break up.
Named (surname only) in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; his mortuary handled the remains of a revenue agent found dead near a moonshiner's still.

Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; developed a commercial fish hatchery in 1920s Creede with Frank Swank, supplying eastern markets with mountain-grown trout. Likely the same extended family as Allen "A.J." and Gordon Hosselkus, also named on this site (the family's Hosselkus Road Canyon Fishery); no relation stated.
Named in the Introduction of John's book "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; ran one of Creede's two full-time barber shops alongside Fred "Soapy" Birdsey.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Memories"; waiting for the doors to open with Charles Slaght, Ray Ball, Charles Dabney and Burl McAdams.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a house painter and paperhanger who painted and papered the Jackson family's little white house before the author's birth, and later became the boy's unwitting model for smoking a pipe upside down.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Gentlemen Smoke Pipes" — the same upside-down pipe-smoking detail as Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; "the little painter and paperhanger, who always expected wet weather."
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Twice Around the Barber Pole"; opened a barbershop opposite Al Hibbs’s on Main Street.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the Creede doctor who delivered the author, and who was impatient that night to get back to pulling a patient's wisdom tooth.
Named as "Dr. McKibben" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; helped deliver the author at home, along with a midwife.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Introduction; as "Dr. McKibbin," sent for the author's father when a sheep-herder rode in with a hole in his belly from a blasting cap; cleaned the wound with the doctor's son and the author's father assisting.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; awaiting a wisdom-tooth extraction from Dr. Samuel McKibbin on the night of the author's birth.

Named (by nickname) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; explicitly "no relation" to the author's family, despite sharing the Jackson surname. His unnamed wife, who had given birth around the same time as Mom Jo, wet-nursed the infant author.

Named as "Mrs. Packrat Jackson" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five" — the same wet-nurse story as Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," here noting she fed both her own new arrival and the author "with little effort."

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a carpenter and prospector who lived next door to the Jackson family with his wife Eva, and was the unwitting victim of a Model T Ford prank pulled by the author and his brother Scooter.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inside Plumbing Blesses Creede"; Dad Bill's well beneath an enclosed porch served his and Charlie Matson's households.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Let's Hear That One Again"; his garage was the boys' hiding spot for pelting the Allen sisters' cows with slingshot rocks.

Central to "Echoes from the Thundermug," "So Long to Ed Snow"; the near-sighted boyhood friend turned electronics engineer, garbage-hauling partner, and Vietnam volunteer, remembered here at length through his death from cancer.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "College Recruits"; drinks two quarts of Muscatel with Bob Blackburn the night before Bob's move to Pueblo, and helps revive him in the snow afterward.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Why Dogs Shouldn't Chase Garbage Trucks"; as C. Edward Snow, John's helper on the Creede garbage route, nearsighted and sensitive to smell, who suggested masking it with Tokay wine and gave the Model T a slug through the radiator cap.

Called "Grandmother Lane" in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; drove with Mom Jo and the three Jackson boys the night of the mercantile-block fire, and helped Dad Bill and Dottie Turnipseed care for the dying Charlie Matson.

Called "Grandmother Lane" and "Gram Lane" in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; raised chickens, rabbits, and geese on the Lane ranch, worked as a practical nurse who delivered most of Creede's babies from 1920 to 1940, and produced butter, buttermilk, and cottage cheese from the ranch's three milk cows.

Called "Grandma Lane" in Chapter III of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; delivered a colt when neighbor Witt Thomas's mare went into a difficult foaling in front of the author and cousin Lee Davis, continuing her long service as a Creede midwife — this time to a horse.
Called "Grandma Lane" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; baked fresh bread with home-churned butter dripped over warm slices.
Called "Gram Lane" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Gentlemen Smoke Pipes"; alternated with Dad Bill and Dottie Turnipseed in the death-watch care of Charlie Matson.
Named as "Gram Lane" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Flatus Before Dessert"; a pot of her lima beans and cabbage, eaten before the Barbers' birthday dinner, was blamed for the author's flatulence.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "Who Upset the Thundermug"; appears as "Maude," John's maternal grandmother, cooking at a boarding house while the family lived on Kerber Creek near Bonanza; the story gives no surname or date.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as a relative of the Lane, Jackson, and Davis families who visited from California in a 1928 Buick touring car. Called "Aunt" rather than "Grandmother" by the author, and described as "rather distant both in lineage and environment," so probably not the same person as Anna Maud Woodruff ("Grandmother Lane"), also named in this chapter, despite the shared first name; no confirmed relation stated.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the wife of Uncle Frank Davis (John Franklin Davis); her kitchen and homemade bread and cookies drew frequent visits from the author, and she was photographed with her husband and two of their children, Polly and Nancy.
Named as "Aunt Caroline" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Flatus Before Dessert"; her kitchen was the reward for playing house with Polly.

Named again as "Aunt Caroline" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Geologist Seeks Ore With Fly Rod and Reel"; made sandwiches for a deer-hunting trip that wasn't, at her husband Uncle Frank's order, after the author and Lee Davis's tall tale.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as "cousin Polly," "the pie maker"; daughter of Aunt Caroline and Uncle Frank Davis (John Franklin Davis), per the book's own photo caption. Made the author play house and eat imaginary mud pies once or twice a week. Per family knowledge, her legal name was Anna Maude Davis, called "Polly" throughout her life to distinguish her from her grandmother, Anna Maud Woodruff (later Anna Maud Lane, John Franklin Davis's mother by her first marriage to Robert Davis) — consistent with this site's own Woodruff research. Distinct from this site's other "Polly," Pauline Roberta "Bubbles" Jackson Bates (occasionally called Polly by her husband's family) — the two share the nickname AND are first cousins: per family knowledge, confirmed Jo (Alice Josephine Davis, Pauline's mother) and Frank (John Franklin Davis, this Polly's father) were siblings, both children of Robert Davis and Anna Maud Woodruff, matching this site's own Woodruff family research.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Flatus Before Dessert" — the same mud-pie game, differently detailed, as Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," "Cousin Polly and Mud Pies."

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," photographed as a young child with her parents, Aunt Caroline and Uncle Frank Davis (John Franklin Davis), and her sister Polly, per the book's own photo caption.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the author, Scooter, and cousin Lee Davis would throw rocks on his tin roof until he came out shaking his fist at them.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; an ex-lawman who lived by the lumber shed and once recruited the author and his brothers to help flush a timber rattlesnake into the open, a job they abandoned as soon as they realized what he was asking.
Named as "E.S. ‘Steve’ Pollock" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Costs, Salary Statistics Given"; Mineral County's sheriff in 1924, per a family record his bride found among old papers.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; with her sister Olive, herded milk cows past the Jackson boys' hiding spot and stormed the Jackson kitchen after Joel spooked her herd with a beanie flipper, coining the line "I don't chew my tubakkur twice."

Named as "Mabel" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Let's Hear That One Again" — the same story, differently detailed, as Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," "Allen Sisters; We Don't Chew Our Tubakkur Twice."

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; with her sister Mabel, herded milk cows daily from the outskirts of Creede to pasture at the head of Slaughterhouse Gulch, selling eggs and milk along the way.
Named as "Ollie" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Let's Hear That One Again" — the same story, differently detailed, as Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," there named "Olive."

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a butcher for A. H. Major, introduced to the Jackson boys as "Uncle Herb" and later revealed, to their confusion, to be married to "Aunt Bernice." Not to be confused with the unrelated Herb Hutchinson, also named on this site.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a large, muscular, Lucky-Strike-smoking woman married to "Uncle Herb," who cared for Mom Jo through a bout of pneumonia and colorfully aired her suspicions about her husband and Guy Timmons's houseguest in front of the Jackson boys.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; mentioned only as having brought an unnamed young woman to town, whom Aunt Bernice suspected of "playing around" with Uncle Herb.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a traveling salesman and old acquaintance of Dad Bill's from his days as a clerk and butcher for A. H. Major, whose joking question about the author's parentage left the boy briefly convinced the milkman Frank Bruns was his real father.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; worked alongside Bill Jackson at the Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation's fluorspar mine and mill at Wagon Wheel Gap. Confirmed by Chapter II, "Of Bagpipes, Coasting and Firemen," as the same Alex Duncan already noted on this site as the father of Gordon, Cloy, Hurtha, and James Duncan.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as a Scotsman who moved to a house across the gulch from Frank Davis after the loss of his dog "Odie"; a former Colorado Fuel and Iron Company employee at Wagon Wheel Gap's fluorspar mine, remembered for a drunken bagpipe march that panicked the neighborhood and reportedly caused a milk cow to abort her calf.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; a Scotsman who lived where the Egolfs later had their summer home, and once let the boys hear one short squeak from his bagpipes.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; boyhood sledding parties gathered on the corner by his house.
Named in "Smooth as Silk A'Goin' or A'Comin'," Chapter I of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; one of the three from whom John leased the Holy Moses group of claims in 1953.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; worked alongside Bill Jackson at the Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation's fluorspar mine and mill at Wagon Wheel Gap. Possibly the same extended family as Les Turnipseed and Dottie Turnipseed, also named on this site; no confirmed relation stated.

Quoted in "Third Stool from the Rear," "From the Barrel of Common Sense," page iv: "Never work with a man who wears gloves. He will spend half his time either pulling them on, taking them off or looking for them."

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as one of "the Dooley brothers"; worked alongside Bill Jackson at the Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation's fluorspar mine and mill at Wagon Wheel Gap.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Two," in "Short Stuff"; took twelve licks from Miss Schroeder's belt without changing expression, then asked if she was "gettin' tired."

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as one of "the Dooley brothers," alongside Ambrose Dooley; worked with Bill Jackson at the Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation's fluorspar mine and mill at Wagon Wheel Gap. Disambiguated by key from the unrelated "Red," a Dooley family friend, also named on this site.

Named again as "'Red' Dooley" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Two," in "Short Stuff"; father of Gene and Floyd, took twelve licks from Miss Schroeder ahead of his brother Ambrose.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; courted by both Bill Jackson and Lee Skinner at Wagon Wheel Gap, with Lee gaining the upper hand until Dad Bill's mule-dropping prank on a box of chocolates meant for her.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; owner of the Princess Theatre in Del Norte, summoned from the projection room when Dad Bill and Lee Skinner nearly came to blows over a seating dispute.

Named (first name only) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the companion of a large stranger who nearly came to blows with Dad Bill at the Princess Theatre in Del Norte, before the two men turned out to know each other.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; alongside Dad Bill and Gram Lane, helped care for Charlie Matson through his final illness so that none of Creede's old timers would die alone. Possibly the same extended family as Les Turnipseed and Al Turnipseed, also named on this site; no confirmed relation stated.
Named as "Kathleen (Dottie) Turnipseed" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; played piano at Milton "Tex" Allsworth's for sing-alongs.
Named as "Kathleen (Dottie) Turnipseed" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Gentlemen Smoke Pipes"; alternated with Dad Bill and Gram Lane in the death-watch care of Charlie Matson.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; an English gentleman who served as Mineral County Clerk, and whose two-fingered pipe grip the author tried to imitate. Photographed with his wife.
Named as "Herbert Barnhart" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Costs, Salary Statistics Given"; Mineral County's clerk in 1924, per a family record his bride found among old papers.

Named as "Mr. Herbert Barnhart, the English gentleman," in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Gentlemen Smoke Pipes" — the same two-fingered pipe-grip detail as Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug."
Named as "Herbert Barnhart" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inside Plumbing Blesses Creede"; his mesa well served the Shillings and Comstock families.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "It's There — All You Need Is Shovel, Willing Back"; Lynn Lezotte struck a coal seam digging his water well, coal he reportedly burned in his own kitchen stove; Jack Kehr now lives in his former home, the well long since gone.
Photographed with her husband, Herbert D. Barnhart, in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; first name not given.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; his garage was among the stops on the author's boyhood cigarette- and cigar-butt-collecting circuit of Creede's business section.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic Age Is Five"; his garage was a five-year-old's wonderland — watching gasoline rise in the glass pump bowl, collecting steel marbles from a cast-off bearing, and witnessing the electrified dog-shock prank at the doorway.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part One," in "Gas Was Easy to Borrow"; ran the Main Street gas pumps where "Wick" worked.
Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; Mineral County's judge, who suffered a fatal heart seizure during his morning outhouse visit, complicating the coroner's and mortician's work.
Named as "Judge Homer Kendall" in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," among the regulars at Soapy Birdsey's nightly poker game.
Named as "Judge Homer Kendall" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "The Magic of Barbershops"; a regular at Soapy Birdsey's nightly poker game.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; when firemen chopped a hole in the roof of his burning shack in winter, he came storming out begging them not to put out the first fire that had kept him warm in weeks.

Named in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as the son of Charles Webber; struck in the arm when the author, aiming for the top of his father's delivery wagon, scored a rare long-distance hit in a boyhood urinating contest.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inside Plumbing Blesses Creede"; his deep well with windmill supplied clear, potable water to several mesa homes.

Named (first name only) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; drew the starting line and judged the boys' long-distance urinating contest at Mr. Bessy's mine, "The Bessy's Cabins Olympics." Possibly the same "Les Turnipseed" named elsewhere on this site, though no surname is given here; not confirmed.
Named (first name only) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; the boy whose distance the author's first salvo beat by two feet in "The Bessy's Cabins Olympics" urinating contest.

Named (first name only) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a lower Creede boy picked up for "The Bessy's Cabins Olympics," whose surprise showing in his first urinating contest put the older boys to shame. Disambiguated by key from other Billys named on this site, none confirmed as the same person.

Named (first name only) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a lower Creede boy picked up for "The Bessy's Cabins Olympics" urinating contest, where he marveled aloud at Billy's surprise showing.

Named (first name only) in Chapter I of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; a hoist man at a local mine who, still drunk, woke to firemen dousing his smoking cabin and worried more about the chicken cooking on his stove than the fire itself. Disambiguated by key from Ed Snow, also named in this chapter.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as one of the Duncan siblings — with Gordon, Cloy, and Hurtha — who joined the mesa platoon after their father Alex Duncan moved to a house across the gulch from Frank Davis. Anticipated on Gordon Duncan's own entry before this chapter was built.
Named with his sister Hurtha in Chapter III of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; taught the author a few simple dance steps ahead of a school dance.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," photographed with Charles Lane and Noel "Bo" Roberts in a photo captioned "The Wisdom of Age," credited to N. L. Roberts. Distinct from Charles Matson, also named on this site.

Named as "Gene Thom" and "Eugene Thom" in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; his house marked the start of the mesa's winter coasting road, and, as a barber in the Heinz building, gave the author his first remembered haircut before later becoming Creede's town marshal.

Named again as "Mr. Eugene Thom" and "Gene" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Wheels for Reet"; as town marshal, pulled over Dr. Whitaker's car for the flagrant violation of a dog appearing to drive it.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Hard Water"; installed a water tank with a water jacket and a real cabinet sink, which promptly froze.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Twice Around the Barber Pole"; one of Creede’s three barbers in the author’s boyhood, running a spacious shop in the Heinz building.

Named (surname only) in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; lived near the mesa coasting road and, disliking the boys' snow-and-water jumps, doused them daily with hot coals after a bad spill of his own.

Named as "Billy Barnett" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inside Plumbing Blesses Creede," the only appearance on this site to give him a given name; a well below his house served the Barnett, Shaw, Duncan and Davis families. The same Mr. Barnett named (surname only) in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," confirmed through family knowledge.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Memories"; as "William 'Billy' Barnett," hefting a 5-pound rainbow trout at Wagon Wheel Gap, Colorado, in 1932.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; a former speed-skating champion on Canadian ice, whose name appears on lode location certificates dating to 1889; held claims in the Equity Mine area and over the divide in Spring and Cascade Creeks.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," in "Bernie, Harry and the Blond Bomber"; with Bernie Soward, a longtime friend who struck a rich silver discovery in the "Big Six" tunnel of the Silver Horde Lode in Sunnyside, and who fled Bernie's household on the morning of the thundermug incident.

The thundermug story that gives the book its title is told again, nearly word for word, in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Harry, Bernie & the Blond Bomber" — see the cross-reference note on both pages.

Named at length in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Two," "Respectability Comes Late to Some of Us"; recalled at nearly 80, his decades-long friendship and rivalry with Bernie Soward, the Mercantile Block fire, and a wartime close call abandoning ship.

Named again as Sheriff in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Finding Body Set Off Long Day on Divide"; joined the author in a rough, foggy recovery of a helicopter-crash victim's body on the divide above Spring Creek on June 3, 1963, and was seriously injured — a crushed vertebra — when his own Jeep rolled on the way down.
Named in "'Bernie Folds His Sails,'" Part III of "Third Stool from the Rear"; leased the Silver Horde mine with Bernie Soward in the 1930s.

Named (first name only) in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as Harry Larson's apparent wife, who "always came out second best" in exchanges with Harry; low-confidence identification, disambiguated by key from Bernie Soward's wife, called only "the Blond Bomber" in the same passage.

Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Two," in "Respectability Comes Late to Some of Us"; took Harry by the nape of the neck after the Mercantile Block fire and put him back to household duties.

Called only "the Blond Bomber," Bernie Soward's nickname for his wife, in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug"; no first name given. Central to "Bernie, Harry and the Blond Bomber," in which she attacks Bernie with a household thundermug.

Named again, as "the Blonde Bomber," in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Two," in "Respectability Comes Late to Some of Us"; John's own brief recap of the thundermug fracas already told in full elsewhere on this site.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug," in "Grant Matzen and the Law of Physics"; lived across the street from the Stone Blacksmith Shop with his wife Esther and their children, and starred in a years-long whiskey-and-revenge feud with barber John Van Buskirk that ended with a threat at gunpoint.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as Grant Matzen's wife and aunt to Hendricks "Heinie" Leonard, who spent school vacations with her. No confirmed relation to Toots Matzen, also named on this site.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as Grant and Esther Matzen's son, who teamed with his cousin Heinie Leonard as "the hell raisers," photographed together with their sisters and the Leonard siblings.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Memories"; pictured in Creede around 1926 with Norma Matzen, Mildred Matzen, Dorothy Leonard, Don Leonard and Heinie Leonard.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as Grant and Esther Matzen's daughter, described as one of the "normal kids" the mesa platoon got along with, and photographed with her sister and the Leonard siblings.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Memories"; pictured in Creede around 1926 with Mildred Matzen, Dorothy Leonard, Don Leonard, Billy Matzen and Heinie Leonard.

Named in Chapter II of "Once Around the Thunder Mug" as Grant and Esther Matzen's daughter, described as one of the "normal kids" the mesa platoon got along with, and photographed with her sister and the Leonard siblings.
