Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "The Road Starts Here"; hunted near the author's Spring Creek home with A.J., Kenny and Trent Hosselkus. Presumably part of the same extended Hosselkus family as this site's other entries; exact relation not stated.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Sue Scores a TKO"; began mining for Emperius Mining Co. in the early sixties after a wandering path through Iowa, Panama, France and Germany; a former professional boxer, married to Sue, a former German Marine he says he never fought "in the ring."

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Sue Scores a TKO"; Jim Brink's wife, a former German Marine who "still retains the tone of command in her voice"; able to summon her husband home mid-brawl or mid-argument with a word.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Mother Bee's Tantrum Put an End to Party"; drove from Grand Junction with Bee McClure on a day the author glimpsed them passing on the Lake City cutoff without stopping.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Whistle While You Work"; braved a geologist's wild driving spree better fortified than the author; later got his emergency whistle full of water joining nude bathers under a waterfall in Squaw Canyon, South Dakota, taking two days to sound it again.
Named again in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; arrived at a Freeport office party with Bob Hawkins and Tina Gonzales.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "I Didn't Hear It 'Til It Was Already Passed"; as "David Jones" and "Dave Jones," a geologist "bursting with pride" in Idaho and later leaning out the right side of a vehicle in Colorado after Mexican food.

Named as "Geologist Dave Jones" in "Grounds for Manslaughter," Chapter V of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; held the record among John's colleagues for longest sustained and highest-decibel snoring, unmuffled even by a foam pillow in Billings, Montana.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Married Life and Mining Camps, Part Three," "Bless the Ladies"; a geologist at the Jerritt Canyon, Nev., exploration camp, pranked by the author into believing that shoving a mop handle up her truck's exhaust pipe would fix its rough running. Surname not given.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; prospected upper Red Mountain Creek southwest of Creede for years without a strike, a learned amateur geologist who "enriched the lives of all who knew him with exciting tales."
Pictured in a photograph captioned "Fred Gulzow" in the front matter of "Who Upset the Thunder Mug"; the verse beneath has him telling Jack Fleming "the gold's in Red Mountain, as plain as can be."

Named as "Mountain Man Lou Oppey" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; found rich float on Red Mountain in the early days of the Depression, assayed as high-grade gold ore by Jack Comstock, touching off a mad staking rush; gave one of his claims to the author's father in friendship.
Named as "Louis Oppey" in "'Sure He's Okay, I Saw Him a Couple of Months Ago,'" Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; spent winters alone on the Roaring Fork or at Red Mountain.
Quoted, "richer than bullshit," in "'Chalk One Up for Blackberry,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear," on first sight of the Phoenix claim vein.

Named as "Mountain Man Lou Oppey" in "'Lou Oppey's Snow Bred Red McClures,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear"; planted potatoes in a spring snow flurry two months early, and delivered a bushel of Red McClures to the Phoenix Mine crew that August.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; Creede's resident chemist, assayed Lou Oppey's Red Mountain float as high-grade gold ore. Possibly related to the site's existing Comstock family (Jimmy Comstock and the "Comstocks" of "Winter Like That of Memories"); not confirmed.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; prospected fissure veins near Spar City for years without reaching his bonanza, but achieved fame as a Creede stone mason.

Named as "Peter Weiss" in "'Sure He's Okay, I Saw Him a Couple of Months Ago,'" Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; a stone mason who spent winters driving a tunnel on Palo Alto Creek toward the Emma Shaft, hiring Roy La Font one winter to help break rock.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; drove shallow tunnels in Cottontail Gulch behind Fred Seyfried's home in the late '30s and early '40s, working the Creede Formation's lead-silver ore. Possibly related to the site's existing Heinie Leonard; not confirmed.

Named as "Mrs. Billy Barnett" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; with John and Lena Slater, bought the author's boyhood rabbit-hunting bag, skinned and dressed, at a quarter apiece. Wife of the site's existing Billy Barnett.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; beat the author at arm wrestling at McClures' Cebolla retreat and supervised a rib barbecue there. Possibly related to the site's existing Fairchild family (Byron "Pappy"/"Barney" Fairchild); not confirmed.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the "'Lite' riders of the sky" at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue, and made plain, with Lisa, that the author was not in Jamie's future plans.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the "'Lite' riders of the sky" who rode in for the McClures' Cebolla barbecue.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the "'Lite' riders of the sky" at the Cebolla barbecue, and, with wife Janelle, stayed over to run the electronics for the author and Inez's surprise "birthday" party.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the young women at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue (first named alone as "Janelle"), later named with husband Bob Kukuk running the electronics for the author and Inez's surprise party.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; "a lanky gal from Monte Vista," one of the young women helping at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue. First name only.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the young women helping at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue. First name only.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the young women helping at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue. First name only; not confirmed as the same Laurie as the site's existing Laurie Wardell, Gene Wardell's daughter.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the young women helping at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue. First name only.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the young women helping at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue; with Leck Fuson, made plain that the author was not in Jamie's future plans. First name only.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; one of the young women helping at the McClures' Cebolla barbecue, the object of the author's joking one-glance infatuation. First name only.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; read the author's earlier article complaining that Mom Jo never gave the children birthday parties, and organized a surprise "Happy Birthday" party for the author and Inez in response; later credited as restoring the Wagon Wheel Gap Depot.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; Toni Shaw's son, part of the group that surprised the author and Inez with a birthday party.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; Doug Shaw's wife, part of the group that surprised the author and Inez with a birthday party. Not confirmed as related to the site's existing Ginny Thompson.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; blended, fashioned and decorated the cake for the author and Inez's surprise birthday party. First name only; not confirmed as the same Tina as the site's existing Tina Gonzales, named in a different, Freeport-office context in this same chapter's "Inez Hooks the Big One."

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Birthday Party Comes on the Wrong Day"; with Gene McClure, filmed the home movies of old Creede stalwarts played at the author and Inez's surprise birthday party.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Which Day Would You Relive?"; promoted the last major mining development at Beartown in the 1930s, remembered for "cracking a mean whip" on Johnny Youngsavage after he wrecked her supply-run Model T. Nickname only.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Which Day Would You Relive?"; became well-acquainted with Johnny Youngsavage in the Creede area working on "Beartown Maude's" 1930s mining crew; later of Alamosa.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Which Day Would You Relive?"; stroked the keys of the old piano at the author's Creede Hotel gatherings, playing tunes inspired by a well-thumbed mail-order catalog.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Anything's Better Than Being Alone"; sent the author a hand-tied gold-ribbed hare's-ear fly made by her son Shane.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Anything's Better Than Being Alone"; fabricated the hand-tied gold-ribbed hare's-ear fly his mother Iris sent the author, which "works."

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Geologist Seeks Ore With Fly Rod and Reel"; the author's district manager and supervisor, who signed his expense vouchers and called to schedule a get-acquainted meeting after a change in management.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Helicopter Pilot Got Even With Big-Shot Passengers"; a large Irish Vietnam veteran who piloted helicopters for a minerals exploration firm, later flying for an exploration outfit in Indonesia; got even with a trio of late, overbearing executives by pretending not to be the pilot. First name only; not confirmed as the same person as the site's existing Pat McKee, a Powderhorn-area rancher named in a different, unrelated story.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; worked in Creede in '76 and '77 during drilling of the Creede formation, and, per his own account, "acquired his bad habits there" — arriving nude to a Freeport office party after passing out mid-change; wife Myrna covered for him and later re-dressed him in a bath towel as "Master 1984."

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; Russ Allen's wife, covered for his absence at a Freeport office party, then re-dressed him in a bath towel as "Master 1984" when he arrived home late and undressed.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; with husband Dave Stevens, hosted a Freeport office Christmas-New Year's party and asked guests to bring their favorite Mexican dish.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; arrived at a Freeport office party with Bob Hawkins and Dave Jones.

Named as "our gal Janice" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Inez Hooks the Big One"; succeeded Jeanne Downing as the Freeport office's administrative assistant. First name only; not confirmed as the same person as the site's existing Janice Nelson, a Cebolla-ranch family friend named elsewhere on the site.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; owned the longest sled among the author's boyhood sledding-party friends, a six-foot Flexible Flyer. Possibly related to the site's existing Edna Ruth Van Aken/Van Akin; not confirmed.
Named, paired with "Bud" Miles, in the roll of "The Top Team Miners" of John's era, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 51.
Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; his home, with Howard Barber's, was a stopping point on the author's boyhood sledding runs.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; one of the "older boys" in the author's boyhood sledding group, who jerked the author's new sled out from under young Jimmy and wrecked its runners on the ice jump. First name only.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Winter Like That of Memories"; left in charge of the author's new sled, cried when Wayne jerked it out from under him and rode it, unauthorized, to the ice jump. First name only; not confirmed as the same Jimmy as the site's existing Jimmy Mason, though both are Creede boyhood contemporaries of the author.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; prospected Spring and Cascade Creeks with C.F. Nelson before their discoveries on Campbell Mountain — the discoveries for which the town of Creede, Colorado is named.

Thanked at length in the Acknowledgements of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," the same closing tribute repeated, nearly word for word, in "Once Around the Thunder Mug" and "Who Upset the Thundermug."

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "Prospectors Were a Visionary Lot Who Built the West"; prospected Spring and Cascade Creeks with Nicholas C. Creede before their discoveries on Campbell Mountain.

Eldest daughter of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, per "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s sister and the author's aunt. Almost certainly the same person recorded as "Lizzie D." (age 12) in the 1900 census and "Lillie" (age 22) in the 1910 census on Billy's own page — this memorial confirms "Lillian" as the name the family itself used for her.

Named as "A. Reudi" in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; daughter of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s sister and the author's aunt. Almost certainly the same person recorded as "Alma R." (age 10) in the 1900 census and "Alma" (age 22) in the 1910 census on Billy's own page; this memorial is the only source found so far suggesting her middle name was Reudi or a similar spelling.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; daughter of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s sister and the author's aunt. Almost certainly the same person recorded as "Agnes E." (age 9) in the 1900 census on Billy's own page. The memorial states only that the family "would lose Agnes... later," without giving a date.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; daughter of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s sister and the author's aunt. Does not appear in either the 1900 or 1910 census excerpt transcribed on Billy's own page, so likely born after 1910; new to this site's research from this memorial alone.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; daughter of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s sister and the author's aunt, who "lost your daughter, Helen, in the waters of Willow Creek." The same drowning is independently pictured in this book's "Memories" section, whose caption reads: "William Jackson House on left and two others were spared. A child, Helen, drowned here in 1906" — the two pages, read together for the first time here, confirm the same event and give it a year.

The "child, Helen" who "drowned here in 1906," per the Stringtown flood photo caption in "Memories"; identified in full via "In Respectful Memory Of" as Helen Jackson, daughter of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; twin son of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, buried as a child "in Bachelor town" alongside his twin brother Francis. William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s brother and the author's uncle; new to this site's research from this memorial alone, with no birth or death year given.

Named in "Echoes from the Thundermug," "In Respectful Memory Of"; twin son of William Thomas Jackson Sr. and Selma, buried as a child "in Bachelor town" alongside his twin brother Fred. William Thomas Jackson Jr. ("Billy")'s brother and the author's uncle; new to this site's research from this memorial alone, with no birth or death year given. Keyed "francis-jackson-twin" to distinguish from any unrelated same-named person elsewhere on the site.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Acknowledgements; one of the two "good friends and co-workers" (with Lynn "Key" Lezotte) to whom John dedicates the collection, who "left us several years ago." Not named elsewhere on this site.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "The Con Boss Conned"; pictured in a photograph captioned "Monte Jay Larson," with the couplet "A dangerous load for the tunnel crew but our motorman will see it through." The story itself does not name him.
Named as "Monte Jay" in an untitled barroom vignette, Part IV of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 41; saw a runaway ore motor and thought it would knock down the whole ore bin.

Named in a front-matter photo caption in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," "Frankie Davis and Paul Snyder Clean the Cars." "Please Go to Hell" and "Echoes from the Thundermug" name Frankie's Amethyst Mine leasing partner as Paul Murray; whether Snyder is a second partner or a slip for Murray is not settled, and the caption is kept as printed.
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Introduction; the first cabin on the left entering Creede from the west; watchman for the Sulphur Mill, who "could speak the Ute tongue very well."

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Introduction; wife of John "Hoot" Owsley; fished trout with him in a large Studebaker sedan and is pictured in memory in "her ever present bonnet tied with a wide red ribbon under her chin."
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Introduction; named across the street from Hoot Owsley, "fitting his crank to the slot" of his awning in the early-morning ritual of Creede's upper businessmen.
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Introduction; shaded the windows of his drug-store near the firehouse on Main Street in the morning ritual of Creede's upper businessmen.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Introduction; the Creede doctor after Dr. McKibbin, who "disliked adenoids and tonsils" and removed many Creede children's glands in his office over the Economy Grocery.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "Granddad and the Jayhawker"; as "Mr. Comstock," who "operated a small store" at Comstock-Kinney Point of Rocks, west of Creede, where John spent the dime Granddad gave him. No first name is given.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "Granddad and the Jayhawker"; as "Mrs. McKay," to whose place Granddad said he would take a load of firewood when a tourist tried to beat down the price. No first name is given.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "The Con Boss Conned"; mill superintendent for Emperius Mining Company, who hired John one summer for cleanup work at the reduction mill at the south end of Creede and asked him to shovel concentrates full time with Key LeZotte.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "The Con Boss Conned"; as "Bryan," in the assay laboratory with John Gulzow, who named John "Con Boss" and had him cross-sample the concentrate cars. Never given a surname.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "The Con Boss Conned"; in the assay laboratory with Bryan; brought in the sampling tools and showed John how to use them. The book does not say whether he was related to Fred Gulzow.
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter I, "The Con Boss Conned"; hauled ore from the Amethyst Mine for Creede Transportation Company; told John, "if bullshit was money you'd be a millionaire."

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "And This Ain't No Bullshit"; a new hand from an Oklahoma and Texas oilfield family who opened stories with "Now listen up, Pard, 'cause this here ain't no bullshit," and drove nails through a board with his palm. Could neither read nor write, and did not stay long underground.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "And This Ain't No Bullshit"; John's helicopter pilot in minerals exploration thirty years later, who cautioned that "real stories will always begin with...THIS HERE AIN'T NO BULLSHIT."

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "A "Runner" in 66 Raise"; came from Illinois in the '30s to mine silver ore; drove his partners crazy with his unhurried lighting of fuses but always reached safety before the first blast.

Named in "Jigaboo Bowels Out," Chapter I of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; played banjo and guitar with left-handed fiddler Loyd Wanzer for the Saturday-night sidewalk dances that raised money in the fur-lined thundermug.

Possibly the same Howard Midkiff named in the roll of top team miners in Part V, though not confirmed directly; in an untitled barroom vignette, Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 8, cleaned up and put to bed a badly soiled Uncle Bud.
Named, paired with Walt Randolph, in the roll of "The Top Team Miners" of John's era, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 51.

Possibly the same Howard Midkiff named in the roll of top team miners in this Part, though not confirmed directly; in an untitled barroom vignette, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 44, sawed the suspenders off a miner pinned by his own drill as payback for shorted timecards.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "Mr. Lehman Draws a Joker"; as "Martin," Dick Lehman's young partner from near Picher, Oklahoma, whose first and last shift ended when the drill started; the story does not say whether Martin is a first name or a surname.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "Is There a Doctor in the Hole?"; as "Benny," a young tram man whose finger was severed in a hang-up in the upper Amethyst workings; he insisted on going back for his glove because "my finger's in it." Named again as the mishap site in "Fire in the Hole and All Over."
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "Is There a Doctor in the Hole?"; as "Billy," the miner who came to Benny's aid and offered to get him outside where he could be driven to town.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "Fire in the Hole and All Over"; crushed by a chunk of carbonate ore while filling a shaft bucket in the upper Amethyst; climbed to the Sloan Tunnel and was doctored at the blacksmith shop.
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "Fire in the Hole and All Over"; at the blacksmith shop sharpening steel with Art Davis when Walter Waldo arrived hurt; had the first aid kit ready.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter II, "The Big Kentuckian"; a former truck driver who hired on as mule skinner in place of Bill Mathews, bragged he could not be drunk under the table, and watched George, Uncle Bud and Zero empty his pint.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "9 Bells for a Shower"; a "little" Last Chance Mine miner who rang 9 bells, the emergency signal, because he needed the toilet after too much "Paddy's home brew"; the hoistman "Tommy" then urinated on him through the skip grille.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Rocky Mountain Fever"; as "Willis," John's fishing companion on the Rio Grande, who was thrown into spruce cones and grass when a woodtick landed on Gracie; the story says he "doesn't remember such a fishing trip."

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Rocky Mountain Fever"; as "Gracie," who came out of the local beanery to join Willis and John and, per the story, feared woodticks nearly as much as snakes.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Wedding Bells and Chesapeake Retrievers"; introduced himself as Santiago de Montoya, Sheriff of Taos County, and a witness at John and Inez's wedding. Not named anywhere else on this site; the book gives no date for the wedding.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Wedding Bells and Chesapeake Retrievers"; of Del Norte, telephoned John's father with word that the town had traded a Model T truck to his agency for a new Chevrolet and he would hold the Ford for him.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Wedding Bells and Chesapeake Retrievers"; at Swinehart's ranch, with a team of black horses in the corral, chained them to the overturned Model T and pulled it upright.
Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "Why Dogs Shouldn't Chase Garbage Trucks"; was asked by Ed Snow to buy the pair a gallon of Tokay wine to cover the garbage smell.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter III, "A Hot Dog Story"; as "Bill Powell," whose ranch, three miles upstream on the Rio Grande, Ol' Yeller reached "before the fire was under control." No further identification is given.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "I'll Drink to That (Or Anything Else)"; third at left in a bar photograph with Ray Ball, Pete Walker, Archie "Spud" Fellows and bartender Ed Hargraves. Not named elsewhere on this site.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "I'll Drink to That (Or Anything Else)"; as "Ruby," a tall, skinny redhead and the one woman who "came as close as any to joining our fraternity" of drinkers until she "puked all over the bar" and moved to California.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "I'll Drink to That (Or Anything Else)"; as "Winston," an elderly, poetry-reciting gentleman who leased a barber shop and addressed everyone as "Mister"; he "invariably pass[ed] out before I have had my fill."

elmer-let-me-put-it-another-way.name: Elmer (Let Me Put It Another Way)

appearances.label: Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Let Me Put It Another Way"; as "Elmer," who went missing from a Creede dance and was found by his wife in bed with a young woman. No surname is given.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Forest Blows a 10-4"; an old friend of Forest Cadwell and hunting client who arrived with a pair of hand-held radios and answered "This is NC one...double zero...four...four...nine" from under his jacket. Not named elsewhere on this site.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Well! I Wiped It Off On My Apron"; as "Bob," Ikie's good friend who hiked with him from Minnesota to Creede and stayed to eat breakfast on the Nebraska farm.

Named in "Who Upset the Thunder Mug," Chapter IV, "Victor Miller and Noel Oates"; photographed with Victor Miller: "where the ore was blasted by our good friend, Noel." Not named elsewhere on this site.

Named in the class-photo roster "Lookout World Here We Come" in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, top row. The book gives no other identification, and nothing here ties her to the Woodruff family this site documents.
Named in the class-photo roster in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, second row, and again among the unidentified members in the school-band caption.
Named in the class-photo roster in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; top row.
Named in the class-photo roster in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; top row.
Named in the class-photo roster in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; seated row. Possibly related to this site's Fred "Soapy" Birdsey and Mae Birdsey, not stated.
Named in the class-photo roster in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, seated row.

Possibly named again, without the middle initial, as "Mary Johnson" in the Acknowledgements of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," thanked among the students of Professor E. D. Watson; not confirmed the same person.
Named in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, as the young lady under director Thomas Drysdale's baton, her married name given parenthetically as "Lamb."
Named in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, playing saxophone, her married name given parenthetically as "Lehman."
Named in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, playing saxophone; possibly related to this site's Charles Slaght, Irma Slaght, and Hank Slaght, not stated.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; possibly related to this site's Edna Ruth Van Aken, not stated.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; possibly related to this site's Dorothy Workman, not stated.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; possibly related to this site's Charles Slaght and Mary Slaght, not stated.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter.

Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; the book gives no relation to Les Turnipseed or other Turnipseeds documented on this site.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter.
Named among the unidentified band members in the school-band caption in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter; possibly related to this site's Stanley Weaver and Woodrow Weaver, not stated.

Named in the Acknowledgements of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," credited (or blamed) with leading John astray "a couple of times." Not confirmed related to this site's other Snows, including a "Frosty and June Snow of Lynnwood, Washington" named among the contributors to John's mock 1984 campaign in "Thundermug for President," Chapter V, below.

Named in the Introduction of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; the Congregational Church minister whose remark, "In truth, there is little difference between man and woman," draws Charles Steele's reply, "Praise the Lord for that small difference."

Named in the caption to the Whiskey Drinking Contest photograph in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," front matter, "holding trophy"; possibly the "Slim" of the "Creede Running Crew" named in "Jigaboo Bowels Out" and "Strung Out to String Up," Chapter I, though the stories give only first names.
Credited for the front cover illustration of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," a pen-and-ink cutaway drawing of a two-story outhouse scene, reprinted again inside the front cover.

Credited for the front cover illustration of "Third Stool from the Rear," a color cartoon of a bartender swinging a rolling pin at two brawling barstool patrons; the same illustration, in black-and-white line art, is printed again with a vignette on page 33.

Credited as "Illustration by Joel Tankersley" under eight cartoons in "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," in Chapters I, II, III, IV, and VI; possibly related to this site's Seth E. "Tank" Tankersley or Joan Tankersley, not stated.

Named in "Jigaboo Bowels Out," Chapter I of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; a left-handed fiddle player in the Saturday-night sidewalk dances of the Depression years. Distinct from this site's Charles Wanzer, not stated to be related.

Named in "'Fiddling Around with the Judge,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear"; a left-handed fiddle player and war veteran who was pummeling a bulldozer operator in a Main Street brawl on election night, 1948, when reminded by John Van Buskirk that he was the duly elected Judge of Mineral County.
Named in "Jigaboo Bowels Out," Chapter I of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; his cafe was one of the landmarks between which the sidewalk dances took place.

Named in "Smooth as Silk A'Goin' or A'Comin'," Chapter I of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," in a comparison to John's bride's reaction after finding a mouse in the water tank: "as pale and shaky as Wylie Turnquist when he learned his girlfriend had flunked the rabbit test." The variant of this story in "Echoes from the Thundermug" names Les Turnipseed in the same comparison, in a different predicament, so the two versions are not naming the same event. Not the same person as this site's Newt Turnquist of Union Supply Company; no relation is stated.

Named in "Smooth as Silk A'Goin' or A'Comin'," Chapter I of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; one of the three, with Allen Hosselkus and Alex Duncan, from whom John leased the Holy Moses group of claims in 1953.

Named in "A Nodding Acquaintance," Chapter IV of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; Seth E. "Tank" Tankersley's young double-jack partner, who struck him between the eyes after a miscommunicated signal. Not the same person as this site's Gene Wardell; no relation is stated.
Named in "Donald Pioneers a Freeway," Chapter IV of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; the Courtesy Patrolman who found Donald asleep, drunk, at the wheel of his high-centered car outside Del Norte.

Named in "Cold Goose and Warm Chickens," Chapter VI of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; Ed Mahoney's farming neighbor, startled into shooting two barrels of his own roosting chickens after his old dog Rex goosed him with a cold nose in the dark chicken coop.

Named, with his wife, in the caption "1930s Entrepreneurs" in "The Golden Years," Chapter VI of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug"; built one of Creede's first service stations with an electric Phillips "66" gas pump, adding groceries and rental cabins.

Named in "The Golden Years," Chapter VI of "Get Grandpa Off The Thunder Mug," captioned "The Bench Warmer"; a heavyset visiting relative whose "ample posterior" pre-warmed the family's outdoor privy seat on winter mornings in 1930. Not otherwise identified on this site.
Quoted in "Third Stool from the Rear," "From the Barrel of Common Sense," page iv: "I ain't never had much but I guess I never wanted much except a warm house and good friends."

Named in "The Perils of Adolescence," Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; her death in Chula Vista, California prompts John's recollection of teenage courtship with her in Creede before World War II, when her family, the McCarthys, rented from Bill and Bessie Lewis.

Named only as "Brent" in "The Perils of Adolescence," Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear," husband and father of the McCarthy family who rented from Bill and Bessie Lewis; surname supplied from the family name given in the story, not stated for him individually. Silica exposure in Creede's mines left him on an oxygen tank.
Named with his wife Bessie in "The Perils of Adolescence," Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; rented a house on Creede's west side to the McCarthy family for $15 a month during the Depression.
Named in "The Perils of Adolescence," Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; gave John's father a bottle of Dago Red wine, later the occasion of John's own first drinking as a teenager.

Named in "The Perils of Adolescence," Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; visited after word spread of John's teenage misadventure and told his mother Josie, "You worry too much... he'll grow up some day and make you proud."
Named in "'Sure He's Okay, I Saw Him a Couple of Months Ago,'" Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; a lonely bachelor who watched the snow pile up at his ranch on Fir Creek through the winters.
Named in "'Sure He's Okay, I Saw Him a Couple of Months Ago,'" Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; battled hard winters and emphysema from a small cabin near Spar City.

Named as "Mr. Reardon" in "'Sure He's Okay, I Saw Him a Couple of Months Ago,'" Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; found frozen to death partway out of his cabin by milk-route deliveryman Raymond Lane, having been "afforded few pleasures in his life."

Named in "'The Last Straw on the Camel's Back,'" Part I of "Third Stool from the Rear"; sentenced two men, Cal and Robert, to a year and a half in Canon City for a grocery-store burglary of about $50 worth of staples.

Named in "'Chalk One Up for Blackberry,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear"; helped sink a discovery shaft on the Phoenix claim and drove "the only tunnel that ended up where it started," following a semi-circular vein back to daylight; miner's consumption ended his work on the claim, which he urged John's father to lease.
Named in "'Chalk One Up for Blackberry,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear"; rented John a compressor and jackhammer after finishing a gold prospect near Saguache.

Named in "'Chalk One Up for Blackberry,'" Part II of "Third Stool from the Rear"; a "big bruiser from California" who joined the Phoenix claim crew after an elk hunt and hoisted the first fifty tons of ore in five-gallon pails by hand, losing 25 pounds in the process.

Named in an untitled barroom vignette, Part III of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 21; rebuilt an air door destroyed when a runaway ore train hit it, from another miner's remembered measurements alone.

Named in an untitled barroom vignette, Part III of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 24; a powerful miner able to carry a Leyner drill and column alone, breaking in a new hand from a union mine in Nevada.

Named in an untitled barroom vignette, Part IV of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 36; said, per the vignette's telling, to have been born in one of Creede's former brothels, delivered by a madam who served as midwife.

Named in an untitled barroom vignette, Part IV of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 36, recalling the bar where the outlaw Robert "Bob" Ford, killer of Jesse James, was shot to death in Creede in 1892; this is a well-documented historical event, not a family connection, and the vignette itself is barroom color rather than a sourced account.
Named in "'I Just Put a Little Salt on His Tail,'" Part IV of "Third Stool from the Rear"; found a poached bighorn ram, its jaw shot off, on an elk hunt with Forest Cadwell and others.

Named in "'Two Tramps and a Dog from Silverton,'" Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear"; helped John prepare the Midwest Mine for core drilling, with a small dog, Ralph, trained to check for oncoming cars by looking out the compressor building's windows.

Named in "'Two Tramps and a Dog from Silverton,'" Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear"; talked John into letting him drive a 6x6 truck, shifted out of low range against instructions, and rode out a runaway grade to a bone-jarring stop; his late father, "Lee," had died earlier in a mine accident.
Named, paired with Howard Midkiff, in the roll of "The Top Team Miners" of John's era, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 51.

Possibly the same Walt Randolph named in the roll of top team miners in this Part, though not confirmed directly; in an untitled barroom vignette, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 46, ran a raise near a stope broken into by tommyknockers' "forty feet for free."
Named, paired with Paul Davis, in the roll of "The Top Team Miners" of John's era, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 51.
Named as "Alvie" in an untitled barroom vignette, Part III of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 29, driving a raise on the Dean fault with the "Wintz brothers" and Paul Davis.
Named in an untitled barroom vignette, Part V of "Third Stool from the Rear," page 45; traded punches with a barroom rival known only as Woody, once threatened at gunpoint after a nose-breaking loss.
